title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
dek: Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders, but the latter collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
why: A front-line operator from the New York Fed explains Treasury market structure, including empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.
who: Investors, traders, and macro researchers focused on Treasury market structure, the market-maker ecosystem, and fixed-income liquidity.
skip: The first roughly ten minutes of small talk and personal résumé review can be skipped.

points.h: The Treasury market is so big it must attract new buyers
points.body: Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries by the end of 2025, projected to grow by another $26 to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (direct buying and selling of Treasuries, partly through inter-dealer broker electronic trading, partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing collateralized by Treasuries, mainly intermediated by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including price-sensitive high-frequency traders and hedge funds.

points.h: High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
points.body: Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), mostly employing high-frequency strategies and trading on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of electronic cash market trading. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — a large yield swing that no one could explain — which led the official sector to truly understand the growth of PTFs in electronic markets and sparked the IAWG's work to study market structure and obtain better data.

points.h: Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
points.body: Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: primary dealers' balance sheet capacity for intermediating Treasuries has completely failed to keep pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is simply that the stock has grown too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility; in other volatile periods the official sector has observed increased PTF activity. But in March 2020, everyone retreated.

points.h: The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
points.body: All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. This is not new in the equity market, but the Treasury market is largely over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not the case there. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries on their balance sheets, and when the selling wave hit, there was no intermediation capacity left. If counterparties could be matched without going through a dealer, that might ease things. But she explicitly says that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — every incremental improvement helps, though.

points.h: All-to-all is stuck on the lack of counterparty matching
points.body: One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Extend the window to a day, and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible innovation directions, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have this capability. But to date, no case in this area has truly succeeded at scale. She also notes that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need to establish bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — just connect to a central counterparty.

points.h: Off-the-run is 97% of outstanding but a liquidity desert
points.body: Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year bonds, accounting for about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The March 2020 dash for cash selling was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed used TRACE data collected by FINRA for empirical work, and the transaction-level data is only visible to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

Another finding from the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity improves relative to other off-the-run securities. This suggests that part of the off-the-run problem is trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; and as for reducing the number of issuance dates and making individual issues larger, the paper has no definitive conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

points.h: TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
points.body: At a recent TBAC meeting, some members suggested expanding transparency of Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics and transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; they suggested considering publishing transaction-level data for Treasury bills and more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including off-the-run and the TIPS market. Golay says this is interesting because data transparency is precisely the focus of the IAWG's recent work, and it was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally believes small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

points.h: The central clearing deadline is right around the corner
points.body: Golay gives the timeline: the deadline for expanding central clearing in the cash market is this December, and for the repo market it is next June. In scope, the cash market is mainly electronic trading through inter-dealer brokers, i.e., currently uncleared PTF trades; the repo market is the vast majority. In size, $2 to $2.5 trillion in the repo market needs to move into central clearing, while the cash market is in the hundreds of billions. She specifically mentions one exemption: central banks.

points.h: The SRF rename was to remove the stigma
points.body: Last year there were several initiatives to improve the effectiveness of the SRP: introducing another morning operation, raising the participation cap to full allotment, and a change in communication. The purpose of the rename was to clarify that the SRP is just an ordinary open market operation, like pre-crisis repo, and should be used whenever it is economically advantageous, rather than being a backstop that should not be used. Golay says this was the original intent of the SRP, but they found there was misunderstanding. Surveys of primary dealers and the Board's survey of senior financial officers show that these changes increased willingness to use the SRP, making it more able to influence money market rates.
